newsitem.title: USA: Clinton votes in hometown, polls point to victory.
newsitem.headline: Clinton votes in hometown, polls point to victory.

text.p: President Bill Clinton voted at a polling place in his hometown's renovated train station on Tuesday, then joined family and friends to await his expected triumph over Republican Bob Dole.

Accompanied by his wife, Hillary, and their 16-year-old daughter, Chelsea, Clinton cast his paper ballot at just after midday. He smiled broadly and waved to onlookers as he entered the station on the edge of downtown Little Rock, two blocks from the state capitol building.
As he emerged into the bright sunlight after voting, Clinton hugged and kissed Chelsea and exchanged an exuberant high-five handslap with his daughter before entering his limousine and driving away.

A Democratic official told Reuters that Clinton's final internal poll showed him winning 47.2 percent of the vote and Dole getting 37.8 percent. The poll showed Reform Party candidate with 7.1 percent of the vote, and 7.1 percent was undecided.

The official said the poll showed Clinton leading Dole in Ohio by 10 percentage points, in Virginia by four points, in North Carolina by two points, in Florida by five points, in Arizona by five points and in North Dakota by seven points.
If the poll is accurate, Clinton will score an electoral vote blowout since all of those states normally go Republican in presidential races.

The Clintons flew to Little Rock aboard Air Force One at 3:33 a.m. EST (2033 GMT), closing out a grueling campaign season that unofficially began more than a year ago. Their emotional return to a state Clinton led as governor for 12 years followed a late-night rally in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, the last stop on a 20-hour, six-state election-eve barnstorming tour.
"This is the greatest country in human history because we have created a system in which you are the boss," Clinton said in asking voters to renew his contract for four more years.
Enroute to Little Rock from South Dakota, the president and first lady toasted their staff and Secret Service agents who have been away from home so often because of the campaign.

Clinton and his aides also danced the macarena, a loose- limbed Latin line dance that Democrats have adopted as their celebratory war dance. Asked to evaluate the commander-in- chief's performance, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had done the macarena "in a presidential manner."

A top Clinton campaign aide was doubtful the president would achieve his goal of becoming a majority president by getting 50 percent of the vote. "I think we'll be just under it," the aide told Reuters. Clinton won with 43 percent in 1992.

The fate of the Republican-controlled Congress was far from clear. Although much of Clinton's popularity in the past two years can be traced to his opposition to the Republican agenda, it was unclear whether his coattails would benefit fellow Democrats.
"We have a good shot at winning back the House of Representatives but the Senate is out of reach," the aide said.
However another political source said early exit polls indicated the Democrats were doing better than expected in Senate elections.

Little Rock city officials were busy preparing a huge election-night street party, closing off downtown streets around the Old State House -- a large white Greek Revival structure where as many as 80,000 people are expected to congregate.

When Clinton was elected president in 1992 it was on the front steps of the historic building, which once served as the state capitol, where he claimed victory before 50,000 people. He planned to do the same again this year.

Vice President Al Gore and his wife Tipper planned to vote in Tennessee and then fly with their children to Little Rock to join the Clintons in awaiting election results. The Democratic ticket had a substantial lead in enough states that Clinton and Gore were likely to be projected as winners by early evening.
